AI.conclusion: Gal3D provides a practical framework for quantifying intrinsic radial 3D structure and comparing galaxy morphology across cosmological simulations, revealing systematic differences between IllustrisTNG and EAGLE in disk extent, bar strength, and higher-order shape features.

title: AT 2024qfm: a luminous fast blue optical transient at a redshift of z = 0.2267 identified by Lasair-ZTF
comment: Submitted to MNRAS. 11 pages with 5 figures and 3 tables (incl., Appendices)
summary: Luminous fast blue optical transients (LFBOTs) emit from x-ray to radio wavelengths, epitomised by the discovery of AT 2018cow in a host galaxy at 65 Mpc. In the following eight years eleven more have been found, at redshifts $0.075 \lesssim z \lesssim0.34$, plus one identified retrospectively from 2016. Here we present the discovery of AT 2024qfm, classified as an LFBOT in a host galaxy at $z = 0.2267 \pm 0.0002$. Its ultraviolet-to-optical luminosity and rapid 13 day fade closely match AT 2018cow. We describe how the transient was identified in the Zwicky Transient Facility alert stream using a custom filter in the Lasair broker that flags flux gradients over time. Another LFBOT candidate was identified with the same methodology (AT 2024kth). The physical origin of LFBOTs remains debated with no firm consensus, and further progress requires more discoveries, host-galaxy characterisation, and multi-wavelength analysis to constrain theory. We discuss this discovery in the context of Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), whose sensitivity will increase the effective LFBOT survey volume tenfold relative to ZTF, out to $z \lesssim 0.6$, and show that our FastFinder filter could recover such events. We highlight the challenge of detecting their fast evolution with sufficiently low latency to trigger multi-wavelength follow-up that can constrain theoretical models.

AI.tldr: The paper reports the discovery of AT 2024qfm, a luminous fast blue optical transient (LFBOT) at z=0.2267, identified via a custom flux-gradient filter in the Lasair broker on Zwicky Transient Facility data. Its properties closely match AT 2018cow. The authors demonstrate the same filter recovered another candidate (AT 2024kth) and discuss implications for Rubin/LSST, which will expand LFBOT survey volume tenfold to z≲0.6, while emphasizing the challenge of low-latency detection for multi-wavelength follow-up.
AI.motivation: LFBOTs are rare and their physical origin is debated with no firm consensus. More discoveries, host-galaxy characterization, and multi-wavelength analysis are needed to constrain theoretical models. This work presents a new discovery method and discusses the future observational landscape.
AI.method: The transient was identified in the Zwicky Transient Facility alert stream using a custom filter (FastFinder) in the Lasair broker that flags flux gradients over time. Photometric and host-galaxy observations were used to classify and characterize AT 2024qfm, and the same methodology recovered an additional candidate (AT 2024kth).
AI.result: AT 2024qfm is classified as an LFBOT in a host galaxy at z=0.2267±0.0002, with ultraviolet-to-optical luminosity and a rapid 13-day fade closely matching AT 2018cow. A second LFBOT candidate (AT 2024kth) was found with the same methodology. The FastFinder filter is shown to be capable of recovering such events in LSST data.
AI.conclusion: AT 2024qfm adds to the growing LFBOT sample. LSST will increase the effective LFBOT survey volume tenfold relative to ZTF, out to z≲0.6, but detecting their fast evolution with sufficiently low latency to trigger multi-wavelength follow-up remains a key challenge for constraining theoretical models.

title: Radio Properties of Narrow-Line and Broad-Line Seyfert 1 Galaxies
comment: 33 pages, 13 figures, 11 tables. Published in Galaxies
summary: Narrow-line Seyfert 1 (NLS1) galaxies host active galactic nuclei (AGN) with narrow optical emission lines of the broad-line region. This is often explained with a relatively lower mass of the central supermassive black hole and super-Eddington accretion. We compared the radio properties of large samples of NLS1 and broad-line Seyfert 1 (BLS1) galaxies compiled from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. We cross-matched the NLS1 and BLS1 samples with the Faint Images of the Radio Sky at Twenty-Centimeters (FIRST) sky survey at 1.4 GHz and the first and second epoch data of the Very Large Array Sky Survey (VLASS) at 3 GHz. We calculated the radio spectral indices, the 1.4-GHz radio power, and the radio loudness. We found lower 1.4-GHz radio detection rates for the NLS1 galaxies. The median radio loudness values, the fraction of radio-loud AGN, and the median 1.4-GHz radio power are also lower for the NLS1 sample. The median spectral indices imply a slightly steeper radio spectrum for the NLS1 sample than for the BLS1 sample. Comparison of the star formation rates estimated from the radio data and the infrared measurements of the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer satellite indicated that more than half of the FIRST- and VLASS-detected NLS1 and BLS1 galaxies contain radio-emitting AGN.

AI.tldr: This paper compares the radio properties of Narrow-line Seyfert 1 (NLS1) and Broad-line Seyfert 1 (BLS1) galaxies using samples from SDSS, cross-matched with FIRST (1.4 GHz) and VLASS (3 GHz) surveys. NLS1 galaxies show lower radio detection rates, lower radio loudness, lower 1.4-GHz radio power, fewer radio-loud AGNs, and slightly steeper radio spectra compared to BLS1 galaxies. Star formation rate comparisons indicate that more than half of the radio-detected galaxies in both samples contain radio-emitting AGN.
AI.motivation: To understand whether the narrow optical emission lines in NLS1 galaxies, often attributed to lower black hole masses and super-Eddington accretion, are reflected in distinct radio properties compared to BLS1 galaxies. This helps clarify the physical nature of NLS1 AGNs and their radio emission mechanisms.
AI.method: Large samples of NLS1 and BLS1 galaxies compiled from SDSS were cross-matched with the FIRST survey at 1.4 GHz and the first and second epoch VLASS data at 3 GHz. Radio spectral indices, 1.4-GHz radio power, and radio loudness were calculated. Star formation rates estimated from radio data were compared with infrared measurements from WISE to identify the presence of radio-emitting AGN.
AI.result: NLS1 galaxies exhibit lower 1.4-GHz radio detection rates, lower median radio loudness, lower fraction of radio-loud AGN, lower median 1.4-GHz radio power, and slightly steeper radio spectra compared to BLS1 galaxies. More than half of the FIRST- and VLASS-detected galaxies in both samples contain radio-emitting AGN based on star formation rate comparisons.
AI.conclusion: The distinct radio properties of NLS1 galaxies are consistent with their interpreted nature of lower black hole masses and super-Eddington accretion. The steep radio spectra and lower radio power support the idea that NLS1 galaxies differ physically from BLS1 galaxies in their accretion and radio emission properties.

title: Complex Energy-Dependent Behaviour of Quasi-Periodic Oscillation Observed in GRS 1915+105
comment: 13 pages, 10 figures, accepted for publication in the Astrophysical Journal
summary: We present complex energy-resolved properties of quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in the black hole X-ray binary GRS 1915+105 using an observation from the LAXPC instrument onboard AstroSat. Power density spectra (PDSs) are constructed in multiple energy bands and modeled with multi-Lorentzian components to investigate the energy dependence of QPO properties. The QPO frequency shows a modest increase with energy. Dynamic PDS analysis does not reveal clear evidence for time-dependent evolution of the QPO frequency, suggesting that the observed frequency shift is not primarily driven by temporal variability. We perform simultaneous fitting of energy-resolved PDSs and find that a model in which the QPO feature is described by two Lorentzian components provides a better fit. The two components exhibit different evolution in fractional root mean square amplitude as a function of energy. We further examine the phase-lag properties by simultaneously modeling the PDS and the real and imaginary parts of the cross-spectrum and find distinct phase-lag behavior for the two components. Overall, these results indicate that the apparent energy-dependent evolution of the QPO feature may be a result of the presence of more than one variability component.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes energy-resolved quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in the black hole X-ray binary GRS 1915+105 using AstroSat/LAXPC data. The QPO frequency modestly increases with energy, and simultaneous fitting reveals that the QPO feature is better described by two Lorentzian components with distinct energy-dependent fractional RMS and phase-lag behaviors, suggesting the apparent energy-dependent evolution stems from multiple variability components rather than temporal frequency drift.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether the energy-dependent evolution of QPO properties in GRS 1915+105 is a genuine physical effect or an artifact resulting from the superposition of multiple variability components.
AI.method: Power density spectra (PDSs) were constructed in multiple energy bands and modeled with multi-Lorentzian components. Dynamic PDS analysis tested for temporal frequency evolution, and simultaneous fitting of energy-resolved PDSs was performed. The PDS, real and imaginary parts of the cross-spectrum were jointly modeled to examine phase-lag properties.
AI.result: The QPO frequency shows a modest increase with energy with no clear time-dependent frequency evolution. A two-Lorentzian model provides a better fit to the energy-resolved PDSs, with the two components exhibiting different evolution in fractional RMS amplitude and distinct phase-lag behavior as functions of energy.
AI.conclusion: The apparent energy-dependent evolution of the QPO feature in GRS 1915+105 is likely a result of the presence of more than one variability component rather than a genuine temporal or energy-driven shift of a single QPO.

title: Differential Reddening and Extinction Law Analyses of Galactic Open Clusters
comment: 15 pages, 9 figures, 1 table, Accepted for publication in AJ
summary: Extinction significantly affects open cluster parameters and their use in studies of Galactic structure, yet homogeneous large sample measurements of open cluster extinction properties remain limited. Using Gaia-era open cluster member samples combined with multi-band photometry and stellar parameters, we derive color excesses of member stars and provide the homogeneous characterization of the mean reddening, differential reddening, and color excess ratio (CER) at the cluster scale. Differential reddening increases systematically with mean reddening, with highly reddened clusters near the Galactic plane showing stronger extinction variations. Star-by-star reddening corrections narrow color--magnitude diagram (CMD) sequences in 369 of 435 clusters (85%) with reliable CMD-width measurements, and cluster color excess maps reveal small-scale extinction structures. The median CER is compatible with the standard diffuse interstellar medium extinction curve, while the broad CER distribution and its large-scale variations across the Galactic disk likely reflect differences in the dominant dust environments sampled along different Galactic sight lines.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a homogeneous large-sample analysis of extinction properties (mean reddening, differential reddening, and color excess ratio) for Gaia-era open clusters using member stars, multi-band photometry, and stellar parameters. It finds that differential reddening scales with mean reddening, star-by-star corrections improve CMD sequences in 85% of clusters, and CER measurements are broadly compatible with the standard diffuse interstellar medium extinction curve.
AI.motivation: Extinction significantly affects open cluster parameter measurements and their use in Galactic structure studies, yet homogeneous large-sample measurements of open cluster extinction properties remain limited.
AI.method: Using Gaia-era open cluster member samples combined with multi-band photometry and stellar parameters, the authors derive color excesses of member stars and homogeneously characterize mean reddening, differential reddening, and color excess ratios at the cluster scale. They also construct cluster color excess maps to reveal small-scale extinction structures.
AI.result: Differential reddening increases systematically with mean reddening, with highly reddened clusters near the Galactic plane showing stronger extinction variations. Star-by-star reddening corrections narrow CMD sequences in 369 of 435 clusters (85%). The median CER is compatible with the standard diffuse interstellar medium extinction curve, while the broad CER distribution and its large-scale variations across the Galactic disk reflect different dominant dust environments.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a homogeneous characterization of open cluster extinction properties, demonstrating that extinction variations are systematic with reddening and Galactic location, and that cluster-scale dust environments vary across the Galactic disk as reflected in color excess ratio distributions.

title: The low luminosity end of Galactic HMXBs with eROSITA: Establishing a luminosity floor for accreting BeXRBs
comment: Submitted to A&A. 20 pages, 17 figures. Comments are welcome
summary: We present a first look at the Galactic population of heretofore known HMXBs as observed by SRG/eROSITA during its first four surveys. eROSITA's sensitivity of $\sim10^{-13}\,\mathrm{erg}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$, translating to $10^{32}$-$10^{34},\mathrm{erg}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ in luminosity for most known HMXBs in the Milky Way, has thus far never been reached by any wide-area survey instrument. We present the extended log N-log L distribution of known HMXBs reaching down to $10^{32}\,\mathrm{erg}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ using eROSITA, and show the large scatter that can be induced by source intrinsic variability. We present sub-type resolved luminosity distributions, showing that the Supergiant X-ray binaries (SgXBs) and Be X-ray binaries (BeXRBs) occupy different parts of the overall distribution, and reanalyse RXTE/ASM data and MAXI for comparison to eROSITA. The luminosity regime uncovered by eROSITA allows a systematic study of the "transient" BeXRBs, which are typically below the detection threshold of monitors outside of outburst, and whose low luminosity behavior has been a longstanding question. Signatures of stable accretion at low luminosities have been observed with pointed instruments for a fraction of the overall sample, so far. With the eROSITA results, we posit that accretion outside of outburst is likely the norm, since a vast majority (> 80%) of BeXRBs are detected at luminosities at least an order of magnitude higher than expected for the most X-ray luminous Be stars. We discuss the observed luminosity in the context of cold disk accretion and the "propeller" mechanism. We highlight a small subpopulation of "isolated" Be-stars that reach luminosities comparable to the least luminous BeXRBs, hinting at the presence of compact object companions.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first systematic look at the Galactic high-mass X-ray binary (HMXB) population as observed by SRG/eROSITA over its first four surveys. eROSITA's unprecedented sensitivity (~10^-13 erg s^-1 cm^-2) allows detection of HMXBs down to luminosities of 10^32 erg s^-1, enabling extended log N-log L distributions and sub-type resolved luminosity distributions of SgXBs and BeXRBs. The authors find that >80% of BeXRBs are detected at luminosities at least an order of magnitude above the most X-ray luminous Be stars, suggesting that accretion outside of outburst is likely the norm. They also highlight a subpopulation of "isolated" Be-stars reaching luminosities comparable to the least luminous BeXRBs, hinting at compact object companions.
AI.motivation: To systematically study the low-luminosity regime (10^32-10^34 erg s^-1) of Galactic HMXBs, particularly transient BeXRBs that have been historically below the detection threshold of wide-area monitoring instruments outside of outburst. This addresses the longstanding question of whether these sources accrete persistently at low levels or are truly quiescent.
AI.method: Analysis of eROSITA data from its first four all-sky surveys of known Galactic HMXBs. The authors construct extended log N-log L distributions down to 10^32 erg s^-1, generate sub-type resolved luminosity distributions separating SgXBs and BeXRBs, and compare with reanalysed RXTE/ASM and MAXI data. Results are interpreted in the context of cold disk accretion and the propeller mechanism.
AI.result: eROSITA detects the vast majority (>80%) of BeXRBs at luminosities at least an order of magnitude above the most X-ray luminous Be stars, indicating persistent low-level accretion outside of outburst. SgXBs and BeXRBs occupy distinct regions of the luminosity distribution. A small subpopulation of "isolated" Be-stars reaches luminosities comparable to faint BeXRBs, suggesting hidden compact object companions. Large scatter in the log N-log L distribution is induced by source intrinsic variability.
AI.conclusion: Accretion onto neutron stars in BeXRBs outside of outburst is likely the norm rather than the exception, as implied by the widespread detection of these sources at low luminosities. The author's posit that the cold disk accretion and propeller mechanism framework can explain the observed low-luminosity behavior, and the detection of X-ray emission from "isolated" Be-stars hints at a population of systems with as-yet-unidentified compact object companions.

title: Widefield Arecibo Virgo Extragalactic Survey: II. Characterizing the HI properties and environment of the WAVES South region
comment: 16 pages + 4 pages of appendices, accepted in A&A, 14 figures, 4 tables
summary:
Context. Galaxy clusters are extreme environments where interactions with the hot intracluster medium drive rapid galaxy evolution. These processes can result in the formation of optically dark gas clouds, as previously observed in Virgo and other clusters.
  Aims. We investigate the distribution and properties of neutral hydrogen (HI) in two large adjoining regions of the Virgo cluster to understand how the cluster environment influences galaxy transformation. Specifically, we examine the gas content of both star-forming and quiescent populations and search for evidence of gas-loss driven evolution.
  Methods. We cataloged the 21cm HI Widefield Arecibo Virgo Extragalactic Survey (WAVES) South data using visual and automatic source extraction methods. By combining these results with an optically selected sample, we compared the HI properties of WAVES South with the previously studied VC1 region. To probe gas reservoirs below the nominal detection limit, we performed a stacking analysis of radio spectra across the WAVES South, VC1 and VC2 footprints.
  Results. We detected 56 HI sources with a median root mean square (rms) noise of 0.8 mJy, including 50 galaxies, two gas clouds (one being optically dark), and the ALFALFA Virgo 7 complex. Our results reveal a significantly lower detection fraction in WAVES South compared to the VC1 region. Stacking showed no new HI detection at a 0.080 mJy rms with a maximum of 157 stacked objects from WAVES South, VC1, and VC2.
  Conclusions. The lower HI detection fraction suggests that WAVES South is a more dynamically relaxed and evolved environment than the VC1 region. The presence of residual HI in a small subset of early-type galaxies supports a model of dwarf irregular to dwarf elliptical transformation via environmental stripping. Finally, we note a possible evolutionary link between optically dark clouds and recently discovered "blue blobs."

AI.tldr: This paper investigates neutral hydrogen (HI) distribution in two adjoining Virgo cluster regions (WAVES South and VC1) using 21cm observations. It detects 56 HI sources, finds a lower HI detection fraction in WAVES South suggesting a more dynamically relaxed and evolved environment, and supports a dwarf irregular to dwarf elliptical transformation model via environmental stripping, while noting a possible link between optically dark gas clouds and "blue blobs."
AI.motivation: To understand how the Virgo cluster environment influences galaxy transformation by examining the HI gas content of star-forming and quiescent galaxy populations, and to search for evidence of gas-loss driven evolution in two large adjoining cluster regions.
AI.method: The authors cataloged 21cm HI data from the WAVES South survey using visual and automatic source extraction. They combined these results with an optically selected sample to compare with the VC1 region. They also performed a stacking analysis of radio spectra across the WAVES South, VC1, and VC2 footprints to probe gas reservoirs below the nominal detection limit.
AI.result: They detected 56 HI sources (median rms noise 0.8 mJy), including 50 galaxies, two gas clouds (one optically dark), and the ALFALFA Virgo 7 complex. The detection fraction in WAVES South was significantly lower than in VC1. Stacking revealed no new HI detections at 0.080 mJy rms with up to 157 stacked objects.
AI.conclusion: WAVES South is a more dynamically relaxed and evolved environment than VC1. Residual HI in a small subset of early-type galaxies supports dwarf irregular to dwarf elliptical transformation via environmental stripping. A possible evolutionary link exists between optically dark clouds and the recently discovered "blue blobs."

title: X-ray Flaring and Variability in NGC 1275, the Heart of the Perseus Cluster
comment: Accepted for publication in ApJ Letters
summary: NGC 1275 is the central galaxy in the Perseus Cluster. The active galactic nucleus (AGN) within NGC 1275 is notable for its strong and variable radio activity, tied to the production of radio jets that inflate large bubbles in the hot intracluster medium (ICM). High spatial resolution X-ray imaging can separate the AGN from the bright ICM, but monitoring the mass accretion rate onto the black hole and establishing disk-jet connections in NGC 1275 requires a high cadence. Here, we report on X-ray monitoring of NGC 1275 using data taken over 20 years with the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory. Modeling the temporally constant ICM in each observation allows X-ray emission from accretion onto the black hole to be traced reliably, with typical flux errors of $\sim 3\%$. X-ray flaring by a factor of $\sim2$ over mere days is detected starting on MJD 59956 (2023 Feb. 21). The flares imply an emission region consistent with $r \leq 870~(10^{8}~M_{\odot}/M_{BH})~ GM/c^{2}$. The profile of the flaring is inconsistent with simple predictions for tidal disruption events. A flare appears roughly 300 days later in radio monitoring data at 43 GHz. Overall, our results indicate that coordinated, moderate-resolution X-ray imaging and radio monitoring could potentially trace disk-jet connections in the AGN that most vividly impact large-scale structure, and be extended to other sources that impact their hosts.

AI.motivation: While high spatial resolution X-ray imaging can separate the AGN from the bright intracluster medium (ICM), monitoring the mass accretion rate onto the black hole and establishing disk-jet connections in NGC 1275 requires high cadence observations that have been lacking.
AI.method: The authors use 20 years of Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory X-ray data, modeling the temporally constant ICM in each observation to reliably trace X-ray emission from accretion onto the black hole, achieving typical flux errors of ~3%.
AI.result: X-ray flaring by a factor of ~2 over days is detected starting MJD 59956 (2023 Feb 21), implying an emission region r ≤ 870 (10^8 M_sun/M_BH) GM/c^2. The flare profile is inconsistent with simple tidal disruption event predictions. A radio flare appears ~300 days later at 43 GHz.
AI.conclusion: Coordinated, moderate-resolution X-ray imaging and radio monitoring can potentially trace disk-jet connections in AGN that impact large-scale structure, and this approach could be extended to other sources affecting their hosts.

title: Radio Monitoring of Classical Novae using the ASKAP Variable and Slow Transients Survey
summary: We present a search for radio emission from classical novae at 887.5 MHz using data from the Australian SKA Pathfinder Variable And Slow Transient (VAST) survey. We cross-matched 43 optically discovered classical novae that erupted between 2021 September and 2025 November within the 1200-square-degree Galactic survey footprint, and found three which show significant radio emission: V6598 Sgr, V1716 Sco, and V1723 Sco. To analyse their radio light curves, we use both thermal free-free and non-thermal synchrotron emission models. We fit the data using the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method to constrain parameters, including the ejected mass and ejecta velocities for the thermal models, and mass-loss rate, explosion energy, wind velocity, and filling factor for the non-thermal model. All three novae show evidence of non-thermal synchrotron emission as the dominant emission mechanism at this frequency. We use a broken power law to describe the radial density structure of a non-uniform circumbinary material, which provides a better fit than a standard wind density profile. This strong early-time synchrotron emission is strong evidence of shock-driven particle acceleration, which may be related to detections of gamma-rays from all three novae as well. In contrast to earlier studies that used multi-frequency data to distinguish between emission models, our analysis is based on single-frequency radio light curves, which can still provide useful constraints on the dominant emission mechanism when interpreted with physically motivated models

AI.tldr: This paper presents a search for radio emission from classical novae at 887.5 MHz using the ASKAP VAST survey. MCMC fitting of thermal free-free and non-thermal synchrotron emission models reveals synchrotron emission as the dominant mechanism in all three, consistent with gamma-ray detections and shock-driven particle acceleration. A broken power-law radial density profile for non-uniform circumbinary material fits better than a standard wind profile. Notably, the study demonstrates that single-frequency radio light curves can constrain dominant emission mechanisms when physical models are applied.
AI.motivation: To search for radio emission from classical novae using single-frequency observations and determine whether thermal or non-thermal emission mechanisms dominate, potentially linking radio synchrotron emission to shock-driven particle acceleration and gamma-ray detections.
AI.method: Cross-matched 43 optically discovered classical novae between 2021 Sep and 2025 Nov within the ASKAP VAST Galactic survey footprint. Analyzed radio light curves with thermal free-free and non-thermal synchrotron emission models, fitting parameters (ejected mass, ejecta velocities, mass-loss rate, explosion energy, wind velocity, filling factor) via Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). Used a broken power law for radial density structure of non-uniform circumbinary material.
AI.result: Three novae (V6598 Sgr, V1716 Sco, V1723 Sco) showed significant radio emission. All three exhibited non-thermal synchrotron emission as the dominant mechanism at 887.5 MHz. The broken power-law density profile provided better fits than standard wind profiles. Strong early-time synchrotron emission correlates with gamma-ray detections from all three novae.
AI.conclusion: Single-frequency radio light curves can provide useful constraints on the dominant emission mechanism in classical novae when interpreted with physically motivated models. The observed synchrotron emission is strong evidence of shock-driven particle acceleration, possibly related to gamma-ray emission.
